{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"553b4ac96d81ea33b860ec761aced2fc42639c0d2034c002bbb4cbc97391a6b2","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:32","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Rules of the road: lights, speed, following, required stops and right-of-way","heading":"C — Rules of the road, part one: officers, headlights, speed limits and the basic speed rule, following and stopping distances, stops required by law, railroad crossings, school buses, intersections and right-of-way","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Rules of the road, part one: officers, headlights, speed limits and the basic speed rule, following and stopping distances, stops required by law, railroad crossings, school buses, intersections and right-of-way
Knowledge domain: the first half of the Tennessee rules of the road — obeying officers, when headlights are required, speed limits and the basic speed rule, safe following distance, what goes into stopping distance, every stop the law requires including stop signs, railroad crossings and school buses, how to approach intersections, and who must yield the right-of-way.

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
You must obey a traffic officer at all times, even when told to do something normally illegal, such as driving through a red light behind a funeral procession. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
Headlights must be on from 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
Headlights are also required whenever you cannot clearly see people or vehicles 200 feet ahead, and whenever rain, mist or snow keeps your wipers running. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
Dim your high beams when an oncoming vehicle comes within 500 feet or when you are within 500 feet behind another vehicle. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
Driving with only parking lights on when visibility is limited is illegal, and so is using fog or auxiliary lights alone or when high beams must be dimmed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A02
Driving below a posted minimum speed in normal conditions is illegal, and even with no minimum posted you may not drive so slowly that you block traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A02
You count as a slow-moving vehicle at 10 mph or more below the speed limit, and with five or more vehicles lined up behind you, you must pull off when safe. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A02
The Basic Speed Rule is a safety principle rather than a Tennessee law: your speed must fit current conditions, and driving faster than conditions allow breaks the rule even below the posted limit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A02
Under the Basic Speed Rule your speed must always let you stop within the clear distance you can see ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A03
Unless another limit is posted, primary and secondary state and federal highways have a 55 mph speed limit. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A03
Tennessee's top interstate speed limit is 70 mph, posted on most rural interstate sections, while congested urban interstates are typically 55 mph. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A03
Driving under 55 mph in the far left lane of an interstate is illegal unless congestion prevents it, and the minimum in the right lanes is 45 mph. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A03
Speeding in a school zone is treated by law as reckless driving and adds an automatic six points to your record, which triggers an advisory letter. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A03
Tennessee law sets a fine of at least $250 and up to $500 for speeding in an active work zone. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A04
Brake early, slowly and evenly; braking too hard can make you skid, and sudden stops make it harder for drivers behind you to stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A04
In a car without anti-lock brakes, if you start to skid, take your foot off the brake and steer in the direction of the skid when it is safe to do so. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A04
With anti-lock brakes, press firmly and steadily, never pump the pedal, and steer around hazards while keeping your foot on the brake until you stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A04
Covering the brake, holding your foot just above it for a quick response, is a safe habit, but riding the brake, resting your foot on it, is not. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A04
Most rear-end crashes are caused by tailgating, which also blocks your view of the road ahead. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A05
Under the two-second rule, start counting as the car ahead passes a fixed point; if you reach that point before two seconds, you are following too closely. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A05
Increase your following distance to at least four seconds in bad weather, at night, at interstate speeds and when following a motorcycle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A05
Stopping takes three steps: perception time to recognize danger, reaction time to start braking, which averages about two-thirds of a second, and braking time. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A05
The manual's example shows that at 70 mph a driver who spots a deer travels 128 feet before braking and needs about 418 feet in all to stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A05
At a stop sign you must stop at a marked stop line or before the nearest side of the crosswalk; with neither, stop where you can see cross traffic but before entering the intersection. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A05
Tennessee law defines a stop as the complete end of all movement, and a right turn on red also requires a full stop first. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A06
When stopped behind another vehicle, leave enough room to see its rear tires touching the pavement, giving you space to steer around it if needed. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A06
A rolling stop is illegal and is grounds both for a ticket and for failing the road test. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A06
Drive at a speed that lets you stop before the nearest rail, and do not cross until every track is clear of trains. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A06
When a train is approaching, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks, never on them, and wait until it has passed and crossing is safe. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A06
Trains must sound their horn about 1,500 feet before a crossing, and flashing lights, a lowered gate, a flagger or a visible train all mean you must not cross. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A07
School and church buses, taxis and other passenger carriers for hire, and vehicles carrying flammable, explosive or hazardous cargo must stop at every railroad crossing. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A07
Meeting or following a school or church bus with red lights flashing and stop arm out, you must stop and stay stopped until the arm is withdrawn and the bus moves. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A07
Flashing yellow lights on a school bus mean it is about to stop to load or unload children, so slow down and get ready to stop. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A07
Passing a stopped school bus is a Class A misdemeanor with a fine of $250 to $1,000. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A07
On a highway divided by a median or barrier, oncoming drivers need not stop for a school bus but must go carefully; a center turn lane is not a barrier, so traffic both ways must stop. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec08-F36 | anchor: A08
More crashes happen at intersections than anywhere else, and the manual says intersections are involved in 33 percent of all crashes and 21 percent of fatal crashes. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec08-F37 | anchor: A08
Use the left-right-left rule at intersections: look left, then right, then left again just before moving, and look twice for motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec08-F38 | anchor: A08
Slow before an intersection, be at your slowest just before entering, get into the correct lane beforehand, and never pass another vehicle inside an intersection. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec08-F39 | anchor: A09
Blocking an intersection after the light changes is always illegal, whether or not a sign says so. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F40 | anchor: A09
The law never gives anyone the right-of-way; it only says who must yield, and you must still do everything possible to avoid a crash. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F41 | anchor: A09
In a marked school zone with warning flashers on, you must stop for a pedestrian crossing in any crosswalk and stay stopped until they are across. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F42 | anchor: A09
For a pedestrian with a white or red-tipped cane or a guide dog, or a deaf walker whose dog wears a blaze orange leash, stop at least 10 feet away and do not honk. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F43 | anchor: A09
When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic going straight or turning right, and when entering from a driveway or alley, yield to all traffic on the main road. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec08-F44 | anchor: A10
At an all-way stop the first vehicle to arrive goes first, and if two arrive together, yield to the vehicle on your right; at an uncontrolled crossing, also yield to the vehicle on your right. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F45 | anchor: A10
Pull to the right edge and stop for any emergency vehicle using a siren, air horn or red or blue flashing light, and stay stopped until it passes or an officer waves you on. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec08-F46 | anchor: A11
Under the Move Over Law, on a road with two or more lanes your way, move out of the lane next to a stopped emergency, utility, road maintenance or tow vehicle with flashing lights, or slow to a safe speed. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0069]

Misconceptions: a green light does not let you enter an intersection still holding other traffic; driving under the limit can still break the Basic Speed Rule; with anti-lock brakes you never pump the pedal; a center turn lane is not a barrier, so both directions stop for a school bus; having the right-of-way is never something to insist on.
Mnemonics: thirty after sunset to thirty before sunrise; dim at five hundred; two seconds in good conditions, four in bad; fifteen to fifty from the rails; left, right, left.
Glossary: Basic Speed Rule means the principle that safe speed is set by conditions; covering the brake means hovering a foot over the pedal; rolling stop means slowing without fully stopping; right-of-way means the duty of one road user to yield to another.
Dynamic facts: speed limits, fines, the work zone and intersection crash figures, and the Move Over Law details can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
